Israeli cybersecurity startup Arrakis Security has raised $8 million in Seed funding to build a platform designed to monitor and govern the behavior of enterprise AI agents, as companies increasingly deploy autonomous systems capable of accessing sensitive data, executing workflows and making decisions without direct human supervision. Full list of Israeli high-tech funding rounds in 2026
Arrakis was founded by Tal Baron, Omer Efrat and Ron Shani, veterans of Torq and Palantir, who argue that traditional cybersecurity tools were designed around a world of human users interacting with machines, not autonomous software systems that can make decisions and act independently across enterprise environments. The company currently employs around 20 people. The new funding will be used to expand its research, development and product teams in Israel, strengthen its detection and response capabilities, and accelerate deployments among organizations adopting AI agents.
Arrakis argues that organizations are facing what it calls a “visibility illusion”: companies may know that an AI agent exists and is connected to a specific system, but often lack a detailed understanding of what the agent is actually doing, which permissions it is using, whether its actions comply with company policies and when normal behavior turns into a security risk.
When it detects suspicious behavior, such as unauthorized access to sensitive information, data exfiltration, privilege abuse or unexpected service activation, it can automatically block actions, revoke permissions, suspend integrations or trigger response workflows. “You cannot secure a machine that thinks and operates differently from humans using security tools that were designed to monitor humans interacting with machines,” said Tal Baron, co-founder and CEO of Arrakis Security.

Arrakis Raises $38M to help industrial companies deploy AI agents and expand its platform across Europe, the US, and the Middle East.
The Series A round was led by blossom Capital, with support from Accel as well as other participants including GFC, MainObject, Rerail, Datadog founder Olivier Pomel, Olivier Godement, head of business products at OpenAI, and Cambridge Aerospace founder Junaid Hussein. The funds will be used to triple Arrakis’ team size and bolster its security measures and the capacity of its AI platform, and to fuel its expansion in the European Union, the U.S., and the Middle East.
The new funding will support international expansion, platform development, and workforce growth. London-based AI deployment company Arrakis announced it has raised roughly $38 million to scale its platform, which helps industrial companies inject AI agents into the critical workflows of their operations. The financing round includes a $30 million Series A from Blossom Capital and comes just 10 months after Arrakis raised $7.5 million in a seed round backed by Accel.
Arrakis says its commercial model is closely tied to customer outcomes, with a significant portion of its fees linked directly to the value delivered. The company currently operates from offices in London and Paris and has already signed its first U.S. customer, reflecting growing international demand for industrial AI deployment. As manufacturers, logistics providers, and energy companies continue modernising their operations, demand is expected to grow for AI platforms that can integrate with existing systems while maintaining strict security and data ownership requirements. results.content:
## Arrakis: The AI Operating System for Industry  
Arrakis just stormed out of stealth mode with $38 million in total funding. This includes a fresh $30 million Series A round led by Blossom Capital and a $7.5 million seed round from Accel. The company is valued at $140 million after this round. Founded in January 2026, Arrakis is already making waves.  
The startup’s secret weapon? Forward-deployed AI engineers who work directly on customer sites. This hands-on approach slashes deployment time to weeks—far faster than legacy vendors that take months or years. Arrakis claims its AI system boosts output quality by two to four times while trimming token costs by roughly 70 percent. That’s efficiency on another level.  
Five paying customers are already onboard—including some NYSE-listed enterprises. One client cut procurement cycle times by a staggering 90 percent using Arrakis’s platform. The startup’s fees tie roughly half of their income to performance targets, showing confidence in their results.  
Arrakis sees particular traction with family-controlled businesses. CEO Rafael Quintanilla, a former Accel VP, co-founded the company with three others: Haroun Beltaifa and Romain Fouilland, both ex-Palantir, and Mikhail Galkov, formerly of Delivery Hero. Quintanilla has openly called Palantir a legacy player ripe for disruption. Arrakis aims to be the AI powerhouse that outpaces them.
## Glow’s Billion-Dollar Vision for Endpoint Security  
Glow emerged from stealth with a massive $180 million funding round at a $1.2 billion valuation. Founded in 2025 by Roi Tiger, Omer Singer, Ophir Arie, and Emily Heath, Glow aims to transform how enterprises secure endpoints with AI-powered prevention.  
Roi Tiger, Glow’s CEO, spent nine years at Meta and knows the tech world inside out. He says, “Prevention was always the right answer in security. It just never worked at enterprise scale without blocking the business. AI solves that. The moment we saw what AI made possible, we knew the endpoint could finally be protected the way it always should have been.”  
Glow’s funding round was led by Sequoia, Cyberstarts, Greenoaks, and Redpoint Ventures. The company plans to grow its Go-to-Market team in the U.S. and expand Glow Labs. They’ve already signed enterprise customers across healthcare, retail, and financial services.  
Glow’s COO Emily Heath adds, “Every enterprise wants to move faster with AI. The question isn’t whether they’ll adopt it—it’s whether security can keep up. That’s the challenge Glow is solving.” Glow will showcase its solution at the Black Hat USA Conference in Las Vegas from August 3 to 5, 2026.
## What’s Next for AI in Industry and Security?  
These startups show how AI is breaking out of traditional office software and into the backbone of business: factories, supply chains, data centers, and endpoints. Arrakis plans to triple its headcount from about 15 employees and open offices in New York and the Middle East. The race to embed AI deeply into industrial and enterprise systems is on.  
With Arrakis cutting procurement times dramatically, Omen AI protecting data center lifeblood, and Glow redefining endpoint security, AI is proving it can deliver real-world results fast. These companies aren’t just dreaming big—they’re building the future right now.  
Stay tuned. The AI revolution is speeding up, and these startups are leading the pack.
